div.head: Chapter 19
div.p: For at least the past fifty years up to this year of fifteen hundred and sixty-three in which by the gracious mercy of God we today live, there has not been, and still less is there today, any man throughout all the Indies who has had or has good faith, nor can excuse himself with it, with respect to four things. The first, with respect to the wars waged on our part against the Indians in all parts, places, kingdoms, and provinces of them. The second, with respect to the armed expeditions and raids — which are one and the same as the wars — that by sea and by land, which they called entradas and rancherías, we have waged and are waged today as they were before. The third, with respect to purchasing the Indian slaves taken in the said wars by those who bought them from the very same men who made them. The fourth, with respect to the merchandise that was brought and sold to those who carried on the said wars, such as harquebuses, gunpowder, crossbows, and especially horses, which have proved more harmful to the Indians than any other weapon.

This principle and most certain truth we prove by the following reasons. But for greater clarity it is well to define two terms or words that we shall have to touch upon many times. The first of these words is: doubt. Doubt is, according to Saint Isidore in his Etymologies and the Philosopher and Saint Thomas in book 3 of the Sentences, dist. 17, di. 4, a movement of reason indifferent to both sides of the contradiction, or an equality of contrary reasons; and so a man is properly said to doubt something when he has reasons equal or nearly equal on both sides, such that he does not incline notably more to one part than to the other.

The second word is: who is the one who can truly be said to be a possessor in good or bad faith. That one then is a possessor in good faith and good conscience who does not know that what he holds belongs to another, and does not restore it though he is able to.

That one is a possessor in bad faith and bad conscience who doubts that it belongs to another; and such doubt is firm when it is said also to touch the conscience, if it proceeds from a just and probable cause he has for doubting, in such a way that his mind inclines more to the view that what he holds belongs to another than to the view that it is his own; this is a firm doubt that touches the conscience, as is gathered from the Gloss in the final chapter of the title, in the words "at no time" and from Baldo, in cap. Vigilanti, De prescriptionibus, 2 columna, eodem titulo.

Likewise, that one is in bad faith who doubts and has persons he could ask — learned persons whom he knows to fear God and who have nothing at stake in telling the truth, and whom he trusts to tell it — and does not ask them. Because such a person is obliged to inquire diligently after the truth. Just as if one were firmly in doubt whether the woman he has is his wife or not, he would be obliged not to approach her until he has asked and learned the truth, and if in the meantime he does the contrary, he will always be in bad faith, and thus in mortal sin.

Likewise, that one is in bad faith who does something contrary to the law out of ignorance of it; as if someone believed that a ward under the care of a tutor or guardian had power to sell his property or alienate it in some other way, and bought it from him: such ignorance of the law does not excuse that person, and he is in bad faith. But because bad or good faith consists in the mind or conscience of each person, and cannot in many cases be truly proved, it may nonetheless be at least proved or presumed from certain conjectures.

One of which is: when it is denounced that what is being done is wrong by persons who deserve to be believed with good reason. So in our present case it is to be presumed against the Spaniards who have gone to the Indies and have committed those abominable deeds, both in the unjust wars they call conquests and in the repartimientos that have been described. For from the year ten, when the friars of Saint Dominic went to the island of Hispaniola — persons held to be holy, prudent, and most learned —, seeing what was happening in the oppression and destruction of the Indians, and having learned what had befallen the great multitude of peoples with which it had been populated and how few remained, then in the year eleven they preached against it very openly and boldly and denounced it, condemning everything that had been done and was being done as tyrannical and abominable. The news comes to Spain and the religious in pursuit of their truth. Great assemblies of learned men are held in Burgos, where at that time the Catholic King Don Fernando was residing; and the king judged everything done in those islands to be abominable, and those who according to God's law felt it to be against his law, grieving over the perdition of so many souls and with such cruelty. Of the islands I say, because the devil had not yet entered the mainland. Certain laws and ordinances are made, but they availed little or nothing. All of this was public and notorious in Spain.

Afterwards, the more the Spaniards went on discovering and entering the islands and the mainland, tyrannizing over and laying waste that so great a portion of the human race, the more did religious and clergy of good zeal come forward, crying out to the kings and to those who governed these kingdoms in their name, that they put a remedy, for those peoples were perishing through the greed and ambition of the men of Spain. There were assemblies in Madrid, in Valladolid, in Aranda de Duero, in Zaragoza, in Barcelona, many and great ones, in the year nineteen, and in the year twenty-six in Granada, as was seen above, and in the year twenty-nine, and in the year forty-two where the New Laws were made in Valladolid and afterwards in Barcelona and then in Madrid, and afterwards in the year fifty-one in Valladolid again. In these times many great provisions were made by command of the kings and those who governed in their name, especially in the days of the Emperor, whom may God hold in his glory, wherein they prohibited the tyrannical cruelties and laid down order so that the Indians should suffer less harm; because through the blindness that God has permitted in Spain regarding this matter on account of its sins, it was never managed to order it perfectly.

Likewise, in all times there were public disputes in the colleges and in the universities about condemning these devastations of human peoples; they were read as lectures from the chairs; there were writings and responses given by learned men; there were confessors who refused to hear confession or to absolve those who wished to cross to the Indies or those who came back from there with money. And all of this was public and notorious throughout all Spain, and it was cried out almost in the public squares that all the money that came from the Indies was stolen; there was no one who was ignorant that royal provisions were issued each day in favor of the Indians and in check and relief of the torments and injustices and hellish life they were given; and as soon as these provisions came to the knowledge of the Spaniards, they blasphemed the King's Council, saying that its members did not know what they were providing and ordering, and by every way and means they could they impeded them so that they would not be carried out, until they utterly lost the shame and fidelity they owed to their king, and rose up killing his viceroy — a man faithful to God and to the king — in open battle. And finally it has been determined by the most learned theologians of Spain, both clergy and friars, that the deeds the Spaniards have done in the Indies are not those of men but of devils; and that everything that comes from there is iniquitously and detestably gained; at the very least no one doubts that it is not doubtful and that there is a presumption of injustice in everything brought from there. Therefore, this was at least probable doubt that obliged all those who wished to go to the Indies to inquire and learn the truth, asking the most devout servants of God and the most learned persons they could find before crossing to those parts: "For it is established that to honest and upright men we give credit more strongly and quickly, not only in those things which are certain and thoroughly known but in general in those which are asserted on either side and rest on judgment of opinion," according to the Philosopher, Rhetoric 1, chapter 3. They were therefore at fault, either of affected ignorance which aggravates the sin if they left it knowingly and out of malice, or of crass and willful ignorance which excuses neither from sin nor from the restitution that must be made; and consequently they had not good but bad faith. Because while they were in this doubt, they were obliged to abstain from all those deeds and from participation in the money and riches derived from them and through them and acquired with them, so as not to put themselves by so doing in danger of sinning mortally. If it should afterwards appear unjust to trade in the goods of others against the will of their owners, despoiled and unjustly wronged, oppressed and killed, and the living thrust into tyrannical servitude: for it is a rule of holy and unholy theologians and jurists alike that, in cases of doubt, if one side is safe and the other dangerous, the safe side must of necessity be followed so as not to expose oneself to such danger; for "he who loves danger will perish in it," Ecclesiasticus 3, and consequently those persons, even if they did not themselves commit the said iniquitous and cruel deeds, if they shared in the goods obtained through them in any manner of participation whatsoever, did not have and do not have good faith but bad faith, and were and are possessors in bad faith and bad conscience.
